title: Linux LVM and Storage Management
description: Manage logical volumes, inspect disk usage, mount filesystems, and work with block devices using LVM and standard storage tools.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, util-linux lsblk is installed and sysfs and the udev database are available to your ordinary account. Use lsblk to list the default set of available block devices, including their partitions, as a tree with mount points; do not restrict the listing to one device.
tasks.explanation: lsblk reads sysfs and udev information and normally prints a device tree with mount points; -f adds filesystem information while retaining the tree. This listing needs no sudo under the stated udev assumption. Default lsblk excludes RAM disks; -l flattens the tree and -d omits dependent devices such as partitions.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, GNU df is installed and mounted-filesystem information is accessible to your ordinary account. Use df to report its usual mounted-filesystem space usage in human-readable powers-of-1024 units, without restricting it to one path.
tasks.explanation: df -h reports total, used and available space for its usual mounted-filesystem listing, with sizes scaled by powers of 1024 (for example KiB, MiB and GiB). It needs no sudo here. -H or --si instead uses powers of 1000; -i reports inode counts rather than block space. df measures filesystem space, while du estimates usage of files and directories.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, GNU du is installed. /var/log exists with nested directories that your ordinary account cannot traverse; root can traverse them. You have sudo access. Use sudo and du to report one total of allocated disk space for /var/log including its contents, in human-readable powers-of-1024 units.
tasks.explanation: du -s gives one total including subdirectories, and -h scales allocated disk usage by powers of 1024. sudo supplies the access needed to traverse the restricted log directories in this scenario; readable directories do not inherently need sudo. --max-depth=0 is equivalent to --summarize. Allocated space can differ from apparent file sizes, and du cannot account for an unlinked file kept open by a process.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, LVM2 is installed and configured to scan /dev/sdb. It is an unused, unmounted, empty 40 GiB whole disk with no partitions, filesystem, LVM membership or data to preserve. You are an ordinary user with sudo access and no direct block-device write permission. Use sudo and pvcreate to initialize exactly /dev/sdb as an LVM physical volume.
tasks.explanation: pvcreate writes an LVM disk label and initializes metadata so /dev/sdb can become part of a volume group. It can initialize a whole disk or a partition; this scenario names the whole empty disk. sudo provides the required device access. Initializing a device that holds data can destroy it; this is not filesystem creation and does not yet create a VG or LV.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, LVM2 is installed and /dev/sdb is already an initialized, unused 40 GiB physical volume with no volume-group membership. vg_data does not exist. You are an ordinary user with sudo access and no direct device or LVM metadata write permission. Use sudo and vgcreate with default settings to create vg_data using exactly /dev/sdb.
tasks.explanation: vgcreate creates vg_data using the supplied physical volume, making its allocatable extents available as a storage pool. LVM normally uses 4 MiB extents by default; metadata consumes part of the physical device. sudo supplies the required access. A VG is a pool for later logical-volume allocation, not a filesystem or mount point.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, LVM2 is installed with normal default LV settings. vg_data exists, uses 4 MiB extents, and has at least 10 GiB of free allocatable space; lv_apps does not exist. You are an ordinary user with sudo access and no LVM administration permission. Use sudo and lvcreate to allocate a new 10 GiB logical volume named lv_apps in vg_data.
tasks.explanation: lvcreate allocates the named LV from the VG: -L sets its size and -n sets its name. LVM input units are binary regardless of case, so 10G means 10 GiB, also 10240 MiB or 2560 extents of 4 MiB. sudo supplies administration privilege. This creates block storage at /dev/vg_data/lv_apps; an ext4 filesystem must be created separately before it can be mounted.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, e2fsprogs is installed. The active 10 GiB LV /dev/vg_data/lv_apps is new, empty, unmounted and has no filesystem or data to preserve; /dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_apps refers to the same device. You are an ordinary user with sudo access and no direct block-device write permission. Use mkfs.ext4 or its equivalent mke2fs invocation to create an ext4 filesystem using the whole LV.
tasks.explanation: mkfs.ext4 invokes mke2fs with ext4 selected, writing a new filesystem to the empty LV. With no filesystem size operand it uses the device size. Creating an LV only allocates block storage; formatting creates filesystem structures, and mounting later attaches the filesystem to a directory. Formatting a populated device destroys its previous filesystem and data; this scenario explicitly supplies an empty target.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, util-linux mount and ext4 kernel support are available. The active LV /dev/vg_data/lv_apps contains a healthy, unmounted, writable ext4 filesystem; /dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_apps is the same device. /mnt/apps exists as an empty, unmounted directory. There is no applicable /etc/fstab entry or unprivileged mount authorization. As an ordinary user with sudo access, use sudo and mount to attach that filesystem read-write at /mnt/apps.
tasks.explanation: mount attaches the existing ext4 filesystem at /mnt/apps; it does not create or resize a filesystem. With both source and target supplied, mount normally detects the type and does not require an fstab entry; -t ext4 can select it explicitly. sudo is needed under this ordinary-user scenario. This is a runtime mount and does not make it persist after reboot. -f is a fake operation and does not attach the filesystem.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, LVM2 is installed. vg_data uses 4 MiB extents and has at least 5 GiB free. Its active LV lv_apps is exactly 10 GiB and holds a healthy, unmounted 10 GiB ext4 filesystem. /dev/vg_data/lv_apps and /dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_apps refer to it. As an ordinary user with sudo access and no LVM administration permission, use sudo and lvextend to add exactly 5 GiB to the LV, leaving filesystem resizing for a separate command.
tasks.explanation: lvextend -L +5G adds 5 GiB from the VG to the existing 10 GiB LV; -L 15G sets the equivalent final LV size. With 4 MiB extents, +1280 extents gives the same increase. Without -r, the ext4 filesystem remains 10 GiB even though the block device is now 15 GiB. resize2fs can later grow that filesystem; extending the LV alone does not make the added space available to files.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, e2fsprogs is installed. The active LV /dev/vg_data/lv_apps is already 15 GiB but contains a 10 GiB ext4 filesystem; /dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_apps is the same device. The filesystem is unmounted and has been checked clean with e2fsck. As an ordinary user with sudo access and no block-device write permission, use sudo and resize2fs to grow that existing filesystem to fill the LV, preserving its files.
tasks.explanation: resize2fs grows the existing ext4 filesystem while preserving its contents. Omitting the size operand uses the underlying device size, 15 GiB here; 15G specifies the same result. It does not enlarge the LV itself and cannot grow beyond that device. An unmounted filesystem should be checked first as supplied here; supported mounted ext4 filesystems can also be grown online. -P only estimates a minimum size, and mkfs.ext4 would create a replacement filesystem rather than resize this one.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, LVM2 is installed with its default local-device scanning and report settings. Several initialized physical volumes exist, and their metadata is on block devices that your ordinary account cannot read; root can. You have sudo access. Use sudo and pvs to display a summary of all initialized LVM physical volumes, including their names, volume groups, sizes and free space.
tasks.explanation: pvs summarizes physical volumes visible to LVM, including their VG membership, size and free extents. sudo supplies the block-device access required in this scenario even though the report is read-only. With no PV argument or selection filter, the report covers all scanned PVs. --readonly reads metadata without locking; -a also includes devices that have not been initialized as PVs, which is broader than this request.
